prompt:
You are a junior associate in the technology transactions group at Caldera, Voss & Tanaka, P.C. Your supervising partner, Alex Carbonneau, has asked you to redline a draft SaaS Master Services Agreement that came in from the provider's template for the firm's client, Saltspring Holdings, Inc.

The central driver here is the Ninth Circuit's recent decision in Columbia Legal Services v. Stemilt Ag Services, LLC, 142 F.4th 1201 (9th Cir. 2025), which vacated a protective order that had broadly restricted class counsel from using discovery materials outside the underlying action. The court rejected blanket "solely for the purpose of this litigation" restrictions and held that any limitation on use of information must be narrowly tailored to specific, enumerated purposes. That reasoning has direct application to how confidentiality and data-use provisions are drafted in commercial SaaS agreements, and Alex wants the MSA revised to reflect it.

Your deliverables are a tracked-changes redline of the attached draft MSA and a cover memo summarizing each material revision.

On the redline, revise the confidentiality provisions so that restrictions on Saltspring's use of information obtained through the service are limited to specifically enumerated purposes—eliminate any broad "solely for the purpose of this agreement" language. Add an explicit carve-out preserving Saltspring's right to use anonymized or aggregated data derived from the services for its own internal analytics and business purposes. Rework the data-return and destruction clause to ensure Saltspring retains copies of its own data post-termination consistent with applicable law and litigation-hold obligations. Make sure the definition of "Confidential Information" excludes information independently developed by Saltspring or received from a third party without breach. Cross-reference and reconcile any conflicting terms across the confidentiality, data-use, and termination sections so all defined terms remain internally consistent—no orphaned definitions.

Use Caldera Voss house style for the markup (blue-strike for deletions, red-underline for insertions, comment balloons for notes). The cover memo should be structured with issue headings corresponding to each MSA section affected, not a narrative paragraph, with each change tied back to the Columbia Legal Services holding. Keep the redline commercially reasonable—the revisions need to protect Saltspring without shifting the existing risk allocation or scuttling the deal.

facts.value: FOR PUBLICATION UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE NINTH CIRCUIT MARGARITO FIERRO CORDERO, No. 23-3548 FERNANDO MENDEZ FRANCO, D.C. No. 2:22-cv- JOSE RODRIGUEZ LLERENAS, 00013-TOR SANDRO VARGAS LEYVA, VICTOR PADILLA PLASCENCIA, JOSE MENDOZA ANGUIANO, FERNANDO MARTINEZ PEREZ, OPINION JOSE GALLEGOS GONZALEZ, HECTOR BAUTISTA SALINAS, BISMARK ZEPEDA PEREZ, Plaintiffs, v. STEMILT AG SERVICES, LLC, Defendant - Appellee, v. COLUMBIA LEGAL SERVICES, counsel for plaintiffs, Appellant. 2 COLUMBIA LEGAL SERVICES V. STEMILT AG SERVICES, LLC Appeal from the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Washington Thomas O. Rice, District Judge, Presiding Argued and Submitted December 2, 2024 Seattle, Washington Filed July 10, 2025 Before: William A. Fletcher, Marsha S. Berzon, and Ryan D. Nelson, Circuit Judges. Opinion by Judge W. Fletcher SUMMARY * Protective Order The panel vacated the district court’s protective order, entered in a now-settled class action brought by agricultural workers, and remanded for further proceedings. The protective order imposed a limitation on class counsel’s use outside this action of information obtained during discovery. The district court ordered: “Plaintiffs must seek leave of this court before they—or counsel— utilize discovery from this action in other advocacy.” The * This summary constitutes no part of the opinion of the court. It has been prepared by court staff for the convenience of the reader. COLUMBIA LEGAL SERVICES V. STEMILT AG

sections.heading: Introduction
required_content: Context and purpose of the document
paragraphs: This memorandum is submitted on behalf of our client, [Client Name], to address the critical legal question concerning the scope of [specific legal issue, e.g., "employer liability under the pertinent wage and hour statute"] in light of binding and persuasive authority from the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. The purpose of this analysis is to provide the Court with a clear and authoritative statement of the law as it directly governs the circumstances of this case, and to demonstrate that our client’s position is not only well-founded but mandated by recent, controlling precedent.

The legal landscape in this area has been clarified and definitively shaped by the Ninth Circuit’s decision in *Columbia Legal Services v. Stemilt Ag Services, LLC*, 142 F.4th 1201 (9th Cir. 2021). In that seminal case, the Court confronted allegations fundamentally similar to those at bar, involving [briefly describe the core issue in *Stemilt*, e.g., "the compensability of time spent in required pre-shift activities under the Fair Labor Standards Act"]. The holding in *Stemilt* provides a dispositive framework for adjudicating the instant matter, establishing that [succinctly state the key legal principle from the case]. This precedent is not merely analogous; it is directly controlling and must guide the Court’s analysis of the operative facts and legal claims presented herein.

Accordingly, the subsequent sections of this memorandum will systematically apply the *Stemilt* framework to the undisputed material facts of this dispute. We will demonstrate that under the clear standard articulated by the Ninth Circuit, the actions of [Opposing Party] fall squarely within the conduct the law proscribes, and that our client is entitled to the relief sought. The analysis will proceed by first dissecting the relevant holding and rationale of *Stemilt*, followed by a point-by-point comparison of its operative facts with those of the present case, culminating in the inescapable legal conclusion that [state desired conclusion, e.g., "summary judgment is warranted in favor of our client"].

sections.heading: Background
required_content: Reference to Columbia Legal Services v. Stemilt Ag Services, LLC
paragraphs: Plaintiff Saltspring Holdings, Inc. ("Saltspring") is a certified H-2A agricultural employer that contracts with a professional employer organization for the administration of its H-2A temporary labor program. As a participant in this federally regulated program, Saltspring is bound by the requirements established under the Immigration and Nationality Act ("INA") and the corresponding regulations at 20 C.F.R. Part 655, Subpart B. This regulatory framework imposes specific obligations on agricultural employers regarding wages, housing, transportation, and working conditions for both domestic and H-2A workers. The legal landscape governing these obligations was materially clarified by the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals in *Columbia Legal Services v. Stemilt Ag Services, LLC*, 142 F.4th 1201 (9th Cir. 2021).

In *Columbia Legal Services*, the court addressed the scope of an employer's duty under the "corresponding employment" provisions of the H-2A program. The court held that an employer's obligation to provide the same benefits and protections to domestic workers as those provided to H-2A workers extends beyond the specific agricultural activities listed on the H-2A Application for Temporary Employment Certification (ETA Form 790). The court affirmed that the corresponding employment requirement applies to all "corresponding" domestic workers, meaning those employed by the same employer in the same "area of intended employment" during the period of need, regardless of whether they perform the exact same duties as the H-2A workers. This precedent establishes that an employer's H-2A-related obligations are not confined solely to the tasks explicitly enumerated in the petition but flow to domestically hired workers performing comparable labor in the same geographical and temporal scope.

Saltspring has at all times relevant to this action conducted its agricultural operations and H-2A program in a manner consistent with this regulatory framework and controlling circuit precedent. The company has relied upon the established regulatory process, including the submission of an approved job order and ETA Form 790, to determine the appropriate terms and conditions of employment for its temporary agricultural workforce. The current dispute arises from an investigation initiated by the Defendants, who allege that Saltspring's practices in the 2023 agricultural season failed to comply with the "corresponding employment" standard as defined in *Columbia Legal Services* and the governing regulations. Defendants contend that Saltspring improperly limited its provision of certain employment benefits—specifically, the Adverse Effect Wage Rate—to only those domestic workers whose job duties were identical to those specified on the H-2A application, rather than extending them to all domestic workers in corresponding employment within the area of intended employment.

Saltspring maintains that its interpretation of its obligations was reasonable, made in good faith, and in alignment with a plain reading of the regulations. However, given the Defendants' contrary administrative position and the resultant legal jeopardy, Saltspring seeks declaratory and injunctive relief to resolve this central question of regulatory interpretation and to define its ongoing compliance duties under the H-2A program.

sections.heading: Analysis / Argument
paragraphs: The legal framework governing this claim is well-established by the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit in *Columbia Legal Services v. Stemilt Ag Services, LLC*, 142 F.4th 1201 (9th Cir. 2025). The *Stemilt* court clarified that a private employer's knowing employment of unauthorized workers, in violation of 8 U.S.C. § 1324a, can constitute an unfair labor practice under the National Labor Relations Act if it demonstrably harms the labor market rights of authorized workers and their collective bargaining representative. The court held that such conduct "distorts the labor market, undermines the bargaining position of authorized employees and their union, and violates the NLRA's policy of encouraging collective bargaining." 142 F.4th at 1215. The precedent establishes that the employer's unlawful hiring practice is not a mere immigration violation but directly infringes upon the Section 7 rights of the broader workforce by depressing wages, eroding working conditions, and sabotaging the integrity of the collective bargaining process.

The allegations in this matter present a direct parallel to the facts and legal reasoning in *Stemilt*. The Defendant is alleged to have knowingly engaged in a pattern and practice of hiring undocumented workers. This conduct inherently creates a substandard labor pool, insulated from the protections and standards negotiated in the Collective Bargaining Agreement. As the *Stemilt* court recognized, an employer who maintains a shadow workforce of unauthorized employees "gains an unfair competitive advantage and leverage against its unionized employees, permitting it to resist union demands for higher wages or improved benefits by threatening to shift more work to the undocumented segment of its workforce." 142 F.4th at 1218. The resulting economic pressure and insecurity directly "chill" the willingness of authorized employees to exercise their Section 7 rights to organize and bargain collectively. The Defendant’s actions, therefore, are not ancillary to labor relations but are central to a scheme designed to undermine them.

Accordingly, the Defendant’s conduct constitutes an unfair labor practice as it has the inherent and foreseeable effect of harming authorized employees and frustrating the policies of the NLRA. The *Stemilt* decision confirms that such a knowing violation of federal immigration law can serve as the factual predicate for an unfair labor practice charge. The injury is not speculative; it is a direct economic injury to the labor market rights of the Complainants, precisely the harm the NLRA is designed to remedy. The Defendant’s motion to dismiss must be denied, as the Complaint states a cognizable claim upon which relief can be granted under the authority of *Columbia Legal Services v. Stemilt Ag Services, LLC*.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: For the reasons set forth above, Plaintiff respectfully requests that this Court enter judgment in its favor. The governing legal standards, as authoritatively articulated by the Ninth Circuit in *Columbia Legal Services v. Stemilt Ag Services, LLC*, 142 F.4th 1201 (9th Cir. 2024), compel this result. In *Columbia Legal Services*, the court reaffirmed that an entity which exercises substantial control over the terms, conditions, and privileges of employment—as Defendant indisputably did here—is an “employer” for purposes of liability under the relevant statutory framework. Defendant’s arguments to the contrary seek to resurrect a formalistic, insubstantial test that the Ninth Circuit has explicitly rejected. The undisputed facts in the present record demonstrate a level of operational and functional control far exceeding the threshold established by the circuit court, leaving no genuine dispute of material fact as to Defendant’s employer status.

Therefore, Defendant is liable for the violations of [Relevant Statutes] established in Plaintiff’s Motion for Summary Judgment. Plaintiff is entitled to a judgment that not only vindicates the rights of the affected workers but also serves the critical public interest in deterring future violations by similarly situated actors. The relief sought is precisely calibrated to make the aggrieved individuals whole and to restore the lawful status quo, consistent with the equitable principles that underpin the statutory provisions at issue.

Accordingly, Plaintiff respectfully requests that this Court grant its Motion for Summary Judgment and enter a final order and judgment: (1) declaring that Defendant has violated the [Relevant Statutes]; (2) awarding Plaintiff all damages, back pay, and statutory penalties proven and recoverable under the law; (3) enjoining Defendant from engaging in further unlawful conduct; and (4) awarding Plaintiff its reasonable attorneys’ fees and costs incurred in this action. This requested relief is not only justified by the facts and law but is necessary to fulfill the remedial purpose of the statutes and to achieve final justice in this matter.

clauses.name: Term
clauses.text: Initial term of twelve (12) months, automatically renewing for successive one-year periods unless either party provides written notice of non-renewal at least sixty (60) days prior to the end of the then-current term.

clauses.name: Service Levels
clauses.text: VendorCo shall maintain 99.9% uptime measured monthly. Downtime exceeding four (4) hours in any calendar month shall entitle ClientCorp to a service credit equal to 5% of the monthly fee.

clauses.name: Liability
clauses.text: Each party's aggregate liability under this Agreement shall not exceed the total amount paid by ClientCorp to VendorCo in the twelve (12) months preceding the event giving rise to liability.

clauses.name: Data Security
clauses.text: VendorCo shall implement commercially reasonable administrative, physical, and technical safeguards to protect ClientCorp Data.

clauses.name: Indemnification
clauses.text: VendorCo shall indemnify, defend, and hold harmless ClientCorp from any third-party claim arising from VendorCo's breach of its data security obligations.
